catalog_quote: Secondly, not only is the final mora excluded for the stress assignment determination, but in Kangri, all inflectional morphology is excluded as well. As argued below, stress assignment is done in the lexicon and is always assigned exclusively within the stem of the word (i.e. word root plus any derivational affixes). Inflectional affixes, regardless of syllable shape, are never stressed. Given these constraints, the assignment of stress in Kangri can be stated by the following rules: • Looking only at the syllables in the stem of the word, • factoring in extrametricality, • the heaviest, • or right-most heavy syllable is stressed. • If all syllables are LIGHT, then the first syllable is stressed. ... 4.3.1 Stress the Heaviest Syllable in the Stem. If a word stem contains a single HEAVY or SUPER-HEAVY syllable, then it will always be stressed. ... 4.3.3 Stress the Right-most Heavy Syllable. If a stem has multiple heavy syllables, then the right-most one will be stressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Within the stem only (root + derivational affixes; inflectional suffixes invisible), with the word-final mora extrametrical and syllables classed light (CV with ɪ ʊ ə) / heavy (CVV, CVC) / superheavy (CVVC, CVCC): stress the heaviest syllable; among equally heavy syllables stress the right-most heavy one; if all stem syllables are light, stress the first syllable. Unbounded (no window). Eaton classes it as 'fixed' in Hayes's sense (predictable, non-phonemic). Tone (high or contour from underlying /ɦ/) is realized on the stressed syllable, so pitch is not a dependable stress correlate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only primary word stress is described (no mention of secondary stress found in the dissertation).
new_statements.exceptions: Inflectional affixes are never stressed even when they contain bimoraic vowels (sec. 4.3.5); final-mora extrametricality needed for words like [bə.'ɾoo.bəɾ], ['də̌.ɾəm] (Table 4-5); footnote 31 (p. 56): author's opinion that when all syllables have equal weight the word may effectively have no primary stress and the initial stress observed in all-light words may be a citation-form elicitation effect; causative/derivational suffixes count as stem and can bear stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word stress assigned in the lexicon over the stem domain; data are elicited citation forms from Kangri as spoken in and around Palampur (Kangra district). Author notes no instrumental duration measurements were made.
new_statements.identity_note: Eaton 2008 describes Kangri as spoken in and around Palampur, Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh (glottocode kang1280, ISO xnr); he treats it as a dialect of (Western) Pahari and compares it with Hindi, Punjabi and Dogri. No sub-dialect glottocode needed.

tone_statements.quote: The occurrence of the tone is the most characteristic feature in this dialect. It is significant to observe that each phonologic word has only one lexically significant and contrastive tone. Phonetically the stress occurs with the tone but it has been considered phonemically an automatic predictable concomitant of the tone hence it is not significant and worth notation in the present description. ... Mostly the tone occurs on the initial syllable but it occurs on the second syllable in the following positions: I. Tone occurs on the causal suffix /-a/ ... II. It occurs on the second syllable when a phonologic word is bound with the initial affix ... III. In a trisyllabic word the middle syllable bears the tone: /pojari/ 'priest', /kotara/ 'dagger'. As an exception, the tone occurs on the first syllable if there is the sequence of vowels and consonants in a phonologic word ... IV. Compound words. The words composed of more than one root morpheme bear the tone on the first element of the compound. sources.note: Whole Chapter 4 'Stress' (pp. 48-67): stress is fixed (predictable), weight-sensitive and unbounded within the stem; final mora extrametrical; heaviest / right-most heavy stem syllable stressed; if all stem syllables light, first syllable stressed; inflectional affixes never stressed; tone (from /ɦ/) docks on the stressed syllable, so pitch is not a reliable stress cue; fn. 31 (p. 56) opines that words with all-equal-weight syllables may effectively lack primary stress and that initial stress in such citation forms may be an elicitation effect.
